vignette:
He is a man who carries his day in the set of his shoulders. At thirty-five, he walks into the session room with a slightly labored breath, as if the stairs themselves ask too much of him. He sits on the edge of the chair, hands resting on his knees, fingertips pressing into the fabric as though checking that the chair is real. He teaches special education at a middle school, and his students-the ones with autism, with emotional dysregulation, with quiet brains that refuse to speak-are the center of his world. But lately, when a student drops a book or slams a desk, he finds himself on his feet, heart hammering, before his mind catches up.

The mugging happened eighteen months ago, late October, after a parent-teacher conference. He had stayed late to write IEP notes and was walking to his car in the staff parking lot. The streetlights flickered-they always had-and he remembers thinking he should report that. A man came from behind the dumpster. He never saw his face, only the silver blade of a box cutter catching the light. The man took his wallet, his phone, the lanyard with his school keys, and told him to lie on the ground. He lay there. The man kicked his ribs once, hard, and left.

He lay there for what felt like a long time. When he finally got up, he walked to the hospital holding his side. The ribs were cracked. The ER doctor told him he was lucky. He didn't feel lucky. He felt like the street had swallowed him whole, and then spat him back into a world that looked the same but felt different.

Now, he avoids that side of the school at all costs. He parks in a different lot, even though it adds twenty minutes to his commute. He walks with his keys poking between his knuckles, a habit that feels both foolish and necessary. He hasn't been able to stay after school since. His principal, understanding, assigned a para to wrap up the after-hours documentation. He tells himself he's grateful. But he feels like a failure-the same way he felt when his students had a meltdown he couldn't soothe.

In class, he notices the smallest changes. A student's chair scraping too loudly makes him freeze. A tap on the shoulder from a colleague makes him flinch so hard he drops his coffee. He has started standing with his back to the wall during circle time. He tells himself it's about classroom management. He knows it's about seeing every door and every window.

His sleep has become fragmented. He wakes at 2:47 a.m.-he checked the clock for weeks-with the sensation of cold metal on his neck. He lies still, breathing through the memory, and then gets up to check the locks. He checks them twice. Some nights he doesn't go back to bed at all. He sits on the living room floor in the dark, watching the street through the blinds, waiting for a shadow that doesn't come.

He used to enjoy quiet weekends alone. Now the silence feels dangerous. He leaves the television on, even when he's not watching. He avoids the neighborhood where the parking lot is, which means he avoids grocery stores, the pharmacy, the coffee shop he loved. His fridge is mostly empty. He eats crackers for dinner, standing in the kitchen, listening.

He has not told anyone at work the full story. He speaks about it in fragments, as if the words themselves could cut. "I had a rough night" is what he tells the aide who asks about his eye bags. He is fiercely patient with his students-naming their feelings, validating their fears, teaching them to breathe when the world feels too loud. He cannot do that for himself. When a boy with selective mutism finally whispered, "I'm scared," he felt a crack in his chest. He wanted to say, I know. He said, "That makes sense."

He is single. He dates rarely, and when he does, he finds himself scanning the room, the exits, the faces. He wonders if he is safe. He wonders if he will ever feel safe again. He wonders if the person he was before the parking lot is still in there somewhere, walking without a clenched jaw, hand at ease, not braced against the world.
